fiveeyes: Five Eyes joint guidance on agentic AI, May 2026

Joint guidance from the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand cyber agencies naming prompt injection as a core manipulation vector and stressing that no single safeguard is sufficient. Useful for an executive audience precisely because it is government guidance rather than vendor material. Alongside it, OWASP's Agentic Top 10 (published 9 December 2025, 100-plus contributors) runs from agent goal hijack to rogue agents and carries the running principle of “least agency” — autonomy as a feature to be earned rather than a default granted at deployment.
prodstack: What a production site actually is, and where the real risk sits

A large-scale production facility is not a plant with programmable controllers — it is roughly 1,000 to 1,500 networked tool computers plus a factory-software layer closer to a distributed transaction system than to classic industrial control. Equipment control systems are industrial PCs, often on long-lived or legacy Windows, with vendor control software; behind them sit robot and handler controllers, mass-flow controllers and gas-panel logic. The facilities layer beneath (bulk gases, deionised water, vacuum, abatement, air handling) is where conventional industrial protocols actually live. Above sits the manufacturing execution system, recipe management, advanced process control, fault detection, automated material handling and the metrology and yield data stores. The security-relevant shape: the tools are old and unpatchable but they are also the LEAST reachable layer. The systems genuinely reachable from IT — execution, recipe, process control, yield, historian — are modern applications, and several hold legitimate WRITE authority into the tools. So the production-environment risk is less “exploit a twenty-year-old tool controller” and more “use a designed data path at the factory-software layer to change what the tools do.”
semi: industry OT equipment-security standards — what they cover, and the gap that matters most

E187, Specification for Cybersecurity of Production Equipment, published early 2022; E188, Malware-Free Equipment Integration, published alongside it. OT security standards are voluntary but are increasingly written into supplier contracts, and at least one major manufacturer is reported to require E187 compliance contractually. E188 addresses the installation, field-service, patching and maintenance path — precisely the vector behind the best-known OT malware outage. THE GAP: E188 explicitly excludes the manufacturing execution system, material-control system and factory-provided host systems, and E187 addresses supplier-provided equipment. Neither standard covers the factory-software layer that actually holds write authority into the tools — nor does E187 cover the facilities and sub-floor control layer. So the systems most reachable from IT are covered by neither.
fabincidents: Documented advanced-manufacturing-industry incidents, including the one specific to the enterprise

The 2018 outage at a major manufacturer, reportedly caused by an unpatched tool introduced to the network during installation, is the canonical case — and the chief executive stated afterwards that patching the affected machines required downtime and supplier involvement, which is the structural reason production sites run old software. In 2023 a ransomware attack on an equipment-subsystem supplier propagated commercially to a major equipment vendor. The enterprise-specific and directly relevant: the trade-secret case involving a Taiwanese foundry and a mainland core product venture, and the 2023 PRC cybersecurity review of the enterprise itself. Note also that automated material handling sits in scope alongside process equipment — it is the production environment's circulatory system, and when it stops production stops within minutes even if every process tool is healthy.
recipeintegrity: Recipe data — why integrity matters as much as confidentiality

A recipe is the parameter set for a process step: tool settings, timings, gas flows, temperatures, the accumulated result of years of process development. It is simultaneously the crown-jewel intellectual property the business named, and a control input. The consequence our taxonomy under-weighted: recipe THEFT is an IP loss, but recipe TAMPERING is a yield and sabotage attack — a small, plausible-looking parameter change degrades yield over weeks, is extremely hard to attribute to an intrusion rather than to process drift, and may be discovered only through yield analysis long after the access is gone. That makes integrity monitoring and change attestation on recipe repositories at least as important as access control, and it is a materially different control objective from the confidentiality framing that usually applies to IP.
agentcode: The agent writing and executing code as a vector in its own right

OWASP's agentic list names code execution as a distinct category, separate from supply chain and from tool misuse. The cases: sandbox escape from a code-execution tool; generated code committed to a repository and later built and deployed; and generated infrastructure or orchestration manifests applied to a live environment. This is adjacent to improper output handling but distinct — the output is not merely consumed by an interpreter, it becomes durable infrastructure or shipped software. Published adjacent work exists on security validation for AI-generated orchestration manifests.
